x.t: Lakshya Sen wins his way into a semifinal in Japan
b: [[lakshya|Lakshya Sen]] is a badminton star from India. On Friday he won a big match in [[kumamoto|Kumamoto]], Japan.
He beat a player from Japan in two games. The scores were 21-16 and 21-15. The match took 40 minutes.
Next he plays Alwi Farhan from Indonesia in the semifinal.

o.t: Lakshya Sen reaches the Kumamoto Masters semifinal in Japan
b: India's [[lakshya|Lakshya Sen]] has reached the semifinals of the Kumamoto Masters Japan, a Super 500 badminton tournament in [[kumamoto|Kumamoto]]. On Friday 13 November he beat Japan's Yushi Tanaka 21-16, 21-15 in a quarterfinal that lasted 40 minutes. Winning in straight games means he won the first two games, so no third game was needed.
In the semifinal, Lakshya will face Alwi Farhan of Indonesia, who is the sixth [[seed|seed]] at the tournament.

It was a harder day for another Indian, Kidambi Srikanth. He lost his quarterfinal to Japan's Koki Watanabe, 22-24, 15-21. A day earlier, Srikanth had beaten Kodai Naraoka of Japan, who is ranked eighth in the world.

stories.think: Lakshya and Srikanth both play for India but had very different days. How would you cheer up a friend after a loss?

quiz.q: Who did Lakshya Sen beat in the quarterfinal?

x.t: Bengaluru's new Pink metro line opens its first part
b: [[bengaluru|Bengaluru]] has a new piece of metro line. It is called the Pink Line.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi opened it on Friday. He rode the train with the state's [[chief-minister|Chief Minister]].
The new part is 7.5 km long. It has six stations. The trains run on a raised track, high above the road.

o.t: First stretch of Bengaluru Metro's Pink Line opens
b: Prime Minister Narendra Modi opened the first stretch of the Pink Line of [[namma-metro|Namma Metro]], [[bengaluru|Bengaluru]]'s metro rail system, on Friday 13 November. He then travelled on a train with Karnataka's [[chief-minister|Chief Minister]], D K Shivakumar.

The new stretch runs for 7.5 km from Kalena Agrahara to Tavarekere and has six stations. It is [[elevated|elevated]], which means the track is built on tall pillars above the streets. It cost around Rs 3,470 [[crore|crore]].
At Jayadeva Hospital station, passengers can change to the line that goes to Electronic City. With this stretch, Bengaluru's metro network is now more than 100 km long.

stories.think: How would a metro line near your home change the way you and your family get around?

quiz.q: How many stations are on the new Pink Line stretch?

x.t: Cricket star Harmanpreet Kaur gets her own wax statue
b: [[harmanpreet|Harmanpreet Kaur]] is a cricket star. She led India's women to win the World Cup in 2025.
On Friday she saw a [[wax-statue|wax statue]] of herself in [[jaipur|Jaipur]]. It will stand next to statues of Sachin Tendulkar and MS Dhoni.
She told girls to dream big and aim to play for India.

o.t: Harmanpreet Kaur unveils her own wax statue in Jaipur
b: Cricketer [[harmanpreet|Harmanpreet Kaur]] unveiled a [[wax-statue|wax statue]] of herself in [[jaipur|Jaipur]] on Friday 13 November. The statue will be placed beside statues of two famous Indian cricketers, Sachin Tendulkar and MS Dhoni.

Harmanpreet, a former India captain, led the team to their first Women's [[odi|ODI]] World Cup title in November 2025. Asked how it felt to stand beside Tendulkar and Dhoni, she said, "I am still not at that level."

She said she was sure "this is just the beginning" for women's cricket in India. She compared the win with 1983, when India's men won the World Cup for the first time, and encouraged young girls to dream big and aim to play for their country.

stories.think: If a statue were made of someone you admire, who would it be, and why?

quiz.q: Where was Harmanpreet Kaur's wax statue unveiled?

x.t: A tough day for India's cricket team in New Zealand
b: India played New Zealand in a one-day cricket match on Friday. New Zealand won by 244 runs.
New Zealand scored 333 runs. India were all out for 89.
India are still ahead in the series, two wins to one. The last match is on Sunday.

o.t: New Zealand beat India by 244 runs in the fourth ODI
b: New Zealand beat India by 244 runs in the fourth [[odi|one-day international]] in [[tauranga|Tauranga]] on Friday 13 November. Batting first, New Zealand scored 333, with Will Young making 125. India were then bowled out for 89.

Matt Henry took six [[wicket|wickets]] for just 27 runs. Three of them came in the very first over of India's innings, when Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli and Shreyas Iyer were all out without scoring. An over is a set of six balls bowled by one bowler.
India still lead the five-match series 2-1. The last match is on Sunday at the same ground, so New Zealand can draw the series but cannot win it.

stories.think: What can a team learn from a really bad day, and how should teammates treat each other afterwards?

quiz.q: How many wickets did Matt Henry take?

x.t: A maths guess from 1960 about today did not come true
b: In 1960, three scientists did some maths. They looked at how fast the number of people on Earth was growing.
Their maths said the number would shoot up without end on one day. That day is today, Friday 13 November 2026!
It did not happen. The number of people kept growing, but more slowly.

o.t: A famous 1960 population sum about today got it wrong
b: In 1960, three scientists led by [[von-foerster|Heinz von Foerster]] of the University of Illinois published a paper in the journal Science. Its title was "Doomsday: Friday, 13 November, A.D. 2026". Today is that date, and the world is fine.

The scientists studied estimates of the world's [[population|population]] over the past 2,000 years. They saw that each doubling had taken less time than the one before. If that pattern carried on, their curve said the number of people would rise without limit on this exact day. The dramatic title was partly meant to draw attention to how fast the population was growing.

Instead, population growth peaked in the early 1960s and has slowed since. The [[un|United Nations]] expects the world's population to reach a peak of just over 10 billion in the 2080s, and then slowly fall.

stories.think: Why is it hard to predict the future, even when you use good maths?

quiz.q: What did the 1960 paper predict for 13 November 2026?
a: The number of people would rise without limit
The Moon would come closer to Earth
All the world's ice would melt

x.t: Ancient stone tips may have carried plant poison
b: Long ago, a big lake sat in a place that is now desert. It was in [[saudi-arabia|Saudi Arabia]].
Hippos and camels lived near the lake. So did people!
Scientists found stone tips by the old lake. Some had tiny traces of a poison plant. People may have used them for hunting.

o.t: Ancient Arabian stone points may be the oldest poisoned weapons
b: About 125,000 years ago, a lake of about 340 square kilometres lay in what is now the [[empty-quarter|Empty Quarter]] desert of [[saudi-arabia|Saudi Arabia]]. It was up to 29 metres deep. Scientists studying its old shoreline found more than 5,500 stone tools, along with bones of hippos, buffalo, camels, gazelles and oryx.

Some stone points carried [[residue|residues]] linked to a plant known as the arrow poison tree. That could make them the oldest known poisoned hunting weapons. Traces of resin, plant fibres and wood suggest the stone tips were fixed onto handles.

The study is a piece of [[archaeology|archaeology]] published in the journal Science on 12 November. It was led by Chris Clarkson of Griffith University in Australia, working with researchers from KAUST, a university in Saudi Arabia.

stories.think: What clues could a scientist find on an old tool to work out how people used it?

quiz.q: Which animal's bones were found near the ancient lake?

x.t: Harry Kane sets an England record and scores the winner
b: [[kane|Harry Kane]] plays football for England. On Thursday he played his 126th game for his country.
No man has played more games for England! He also scored the winning goal.
England beat Croatia 2-1 at [[wembley|Wembley]] stadium in London.

o.t: Harry Kane plays a record 126th game for England, and wins it
b: [[kane|Harry Kane]] played his 126th game for England on Thursday 12 November. That makes him England's most-capped men's player. Each game a player plays for their country is called a [[cap|cap]]. Kane moved past the old record holder, goalkeeper Peter Shilton.

England beat Croatia 2-1 at [[wembley|Wembley]] in the [[nations-league|Nations League]]. Morgan Rogers scored first, Croatia's Petar Sučić made it 1-1, and Kane scored the winning goal from a penalty. It was his 92nd goal for England.
The win sends England into the quarter-finals. On Sunday they play Spain in Madrid to decide who finishes top of the group.

stories.think: Harry Kane has played for England 126 times. What is something you would like to keep doing for many years?

quiz.q: Whose record did Harry Kane pass?

x.t: North Korea changes the shape of its flag
b: Every country's flag has a shape. Some flags are long and thin. Some are closer to a square.
[[north-korea|North Korea]] has made its flag a little less wide. The colours and the red star stay the same.
It is the first change to the flag's shape since 1948.

o.t: North Korea changes its flag's shape for the first time since 1948
b: [[north-korea|North Korea]] has changed the shape of its national flag. Its revised [[constitution|constitution]], posted on a state website called Naenara, says the flag's height and width must now be in the [[ratio|ratio]] 1 to 1.65. Before, the ratio was 1 to 2.
That means the flag is now less wide. For every 1 metre of height, the flag used to be 2 metres wide. Now it is 1.65 metres wide. The new rule is in Article 166 of the constitution.

Reports say the central red field, the white and blue stripes and the red five-pointed star stay the same. It is the first change to the flag's proportions in 78 years, since the country was founded in 1948.

stories.think: If your class had its own flag, what would you put on it, and what shape would it be?

quiz.q: What is the new height-to-width ratio of North Korea's flag?

cop: A big yearly meeting where countries talk about climate change.
Conference of the Parties: the yearly summit of countries that signed the UN climate treaty of 1992. COP21 in 2015 produced the Paris Agreement.
turkiye: A country that is partly in Europe and partly in Asia. In English it used to be called Turkey.
A country bridging Europe and Asia. Its capital is Ankara and its largest city is Istanbul. In 2022 the UN began using the name Türkiye at the government's request.
un: A club of almost every country in the world that works for peace and helps people.
Founded in 1945 after the Second World War, with 193 member countries. Its family includes the Security Council, UNICEF and the World Health Organization.
climate-change: Earth slowly getting warmer over many years, mostly because people burn coal, oil and gas.

Long-term shifts in temperature and weather. Since the 1800s, burning fossil fuels has added carbon dioxide to the air, trapping heat. Earth is already more than 1°C warmer than before the industrial age.
paris-agreement: A promise made by countries in 2015 to slow down global warming.
A 2015 treaty in which countries agreed to keep warming well below 2°C and to try for 1.5°C, with each country setting its own targets.
fossil-fuels: Coal, oil and gas. People burn them to make energy.
Coal, oil and natural gas, formed underground over millions of years. Burning them releases carbon dioxide, which traps heat.
yog: An Olympic Games just for teenage athletes.
A version of the Olympic Games for teenage athletes. The 2026 Games are in Dakar, Senegal, from 31 October to 13 November.
dakar: A city in Senegal, a country in the west of Africa.
A city in Senegal, in West Africa, and the host of the 2026 Youth Olympic Games.
philippines: A country in Asia made up of thousands of islands.
A country in South-East Asia made up of thousands of islands, including Luzon and Mindoro.
satellite: Something that goes around a planet. People build satellites to take pictures and send signals.
An object that orbits a planet. Artificial satellites relay phone and TV signals, guide GPS and photograph Earth for weather and maps.
unanimous: Agreed by everyone. In boxing, a unanimous decision means every judge picked the same winner.
patna: A city in India. It is the capital of the state of Bihar.
The capital city of the state of Bihar, in northern India.
chhath: A festival. Lots of people travel between Delhi and Bihar for it.
A festival that brings a seasonal rush of travellers between Delhi and Bihar. This train ran as a special service for it.
indian-railways: The organisation that runs India's trains.
maharashtra: A state in India. Part of it is by the sea.
A state in India. Raigad and Ratnagiri are two of its coastal districts.
konkan: A long strip of land beside the sea in western India.
A coastal plain in western India, between the Arabian Sea and the Western Ghats. It includes the coast of Maharashtra.
blue-flag: A prize for beaches that are clean, safe and kind to nature.
An international award for beaches. It covers water quality, cleanliness, safety, facilities and protecting nature.
biodiversity: All the different plants and animals that live in a place.
The variety of living things in a place, from tiny creatures to plants, birds and fish.
isro: The Indian Space Research Organisation, India's space agency.
cryogenic: A rocket engine that burns very, very cold liquid fuel.
A rocket engine whose fuel has to stay extremely cold to remain liquid. This one burns liquid hydrogen with liquid oxygen.
gslv: Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle: one of ISRO's rockets. Its third stage uses a cryogenic engine.
navic: India's group of satellites that help people find their way.
Navigation with Indian Constellation: India's regional satellite navigation system.
inflation: When prices in the shops keep going up.
A rise in prices over time. It is usually given as a percentage: how much more things cost than a year ago.
rbi: India's central bank. It looks after the country's money.
India's central bank. It is required to keep inflation between 2 and 6 per cent, and it sets a main interest rate.
interest-rate: The extra money you pay back when you borrow money.
The cost of borrowing money, shown as a percentage. When a central bank raises its rate, loans become more expensive.
consensus: When everyone in a group agrees.
Agreement by everyone in a group. If decisions need consensus, the wording must be something that all sides can accept.
emperor: The ruler of an empire, which is a group of many lands.
The ruler of an empire. Rome had emperors, among them Hadrian and Antoninus Pius.
antoninus-pius: A Roman emperor who ruled long, long ago.
Roman emperor from AD 138 to 161. Around AD 142 his army began building the Antonine Wall across Scotland.
romans: People of ancient Rome. They ruled a huge empire long ago.
The people of ancient Rome. At its largest, their empire stretched from Britain to northern Africa.
bronze: A strong metal made by mixing other metals together.
A metal made by mixing copper with a smaller amount of tin.
gilded: Covered with a thin layer of gold.
Covered with a thin layer of gold, so that an object looks as if it is made of gold.
archaeology: Learning about the past by digging up the things people left behind.
The scientific study of people in the past, through the objects, buildings and bones they left behind.
radiocarbon: A way for scientists to find out how old the remains of living things are.
A technique for finding the age of remains that came from living things. It measures a kind of carbon called carbon-14.
bird-of-prey: A bird that hunts other animals for food, such as an owl.
A bird that hunts other animals for food. Short-eared owls and hen harriers are birds of prey.
florida: A state in the United States. It has a coast on the Gulf.
A state in the United States. Destin, Pensacola and Panama City are on its Gulf coast.
artificial-reef: Something people put on the sea floor so sea animals can live there.
A human-made structure placed on the seabed to make a habitat for sea life. Old ships are sometimes cleaned and sunk for this.
ocean-liner: A big ship that carries people across the ocean.
A large ship that crosses oceans on a regular schedule between set ports. The SS United States carried passengers across the Atlantic.
spacex: The company that builds the Starship rocket.
The company that builds and flies Starship. Its launch site in Texas is called Starbase.
starship: A giant rocket with two parts, built by SpaceX.
SpaceX's giant two-part rocket: a booster called Super Heavy and an upper part called Ship. It is designed to be reused.
reusable: A rocket that can fly more than once.
A rocket that comes back after launch so that it can fly again and is not thrown away.
orbit: The path something takes as it goes round and round a planet.
The curved path of an object around a planet or star. One trip around Earth is one orbit.
atp-finals: A tennis contest for the top eight players of the year.
The tournament that ends the men's tennis season. The top eight singles players and the best eight doubles teams of the season qualify.
turin: A city in north-western Italy. It has hosted the ATP Finals since 2021.
round-robin: A contest where everyone in a group plays everyone else.
A format in which every player or team in a group plays all the others, with no instant knockout.
asean: A group of neighbouring countries in South-East Asia that work together.
The Association of Southeast Asian Nations. Its members take turns to chair the group.
manila: The capital city of the Philippines.
The capital of the Philippines and the host of the 49th ASEAN Summit.
summit: A big meeting between the leaders of countries.
A meeting between the leaders of countries or organisations.
chimpanzee: A kind of ape that lives in Africa.
A great ape found across central and West Africa, for example in Taï National Park in Côte d'Ivoire.
ivory-coast: A country in Africa. It is also called Ivory Coast.
A country in West Africa, also called Ivory Coast. Taï National Park is there.
grooming: When animals clean each other's fur.
When animals clean each other's fur, for example by picking out parasites.
sanctuary: A safe place where animals are looked after.
A safe place where animals, such as orphaned chimpanzees, are cared for.
lakshya: An Indian badminton player who competes in top tournaments around the world.
kumamoto: A city on the island of Kyushu, in southern Japan.
seed: A top player who is kept away from other top players early on.
A player ranked highly before a tournament and placed in the draw so the top players do not meet in the early rounds.
bengaluru: A big city in south India.
The capital city of Karnataka state, in south India.
namma-metro: Bengaluru's metro rail system. Namma means 'our' in Kannada.
chief-minister: The leader of a state's government.
The head of the government of an Indian state.
elevated: Built above the ground, for example on pillars over a road.
crore: A very big number: 1 with seven zeros after it.
An Indian unit for 10 million, written 1,00,00,000.
harmanpreet: A cricket star who led India's women's team.
An Indian cricketer who captained India to the 2025 Women's ODI World Cup title.
wax-statue: A life-size model of a person made of wax.
A lifelike figure of a person, made from wax and painted to look real.
jaipur: The capital city of Rajasthan, in north-west India.
odi: A cricket match between countries that lasts one day.
One Day International: a cricket match between countries in which each team bats for up to 50 overs.
wicket: When the bowling team gets a batter out, it takes a wicket.
In cricket, taking a wicket means getting a batter out. A team is all out after losing 10 wickets.
tauranga: A city in New Zealand, by the sea.
A coastal city on the North Island of New Zealand.
kane: A footballer who plays for England.
An English footballer who plays as a striker for England's national team.
cap: One game played for your country.
In football, each game a player plays for their national team is called a cap.
wembley: A huge football stadium in London.
England's national football stadium, in London.
nations-league: A football contest between teams from Europe.
The UEFA Nations League, a competition between the national teams of Europe.
von-foerster: A scientist who did maths about the number of people on Earth.
An Austrian-American physicist at the University of Illinois who led the 1960 population paper.
population: The number of people living in a place.
The total number of people living in a place, such as a country or the whole world.
saudi-arabia: A big country in western Asia with lots of desert.
A country that covers most of the Arabian Peninsula in western Asia.
empty-quarter: A vast sand desert in the south of the Arabian Peninsula, also called the Rub' al Khali.
residue: A tiny bit of something left behind.
A small trace of a substance left on a surface, which scientists can test.
north-korea: A country in East Asia, on the northern half of the Korean Peninsula.
constitution: The most important set of rules for a country.
The main written set of rules that says how a country is run.
ratio: A way to compare two numbers.
A way of comparing two amounts, such as a flag's height and width, written like 1 to 2 or 1:2.

g-nkflag.q: Is North Korea's flag now wider or less wide than before?
g-nkflag.right: Yes! It used to be 2 times as wide as it is tall. Now it is 1.65 times.
g-nkflag.wrong: Not quite. The flag got a little less wide.

g-popmaths.right: Right! The number of people grew more slowly instead.
g-popmaths.wrong: Not this time. The guess was wrong, and growth slowed down.

in-lakshya.ctx: A badminton match is the best of three games, and a game is won by reaching 21 points with a lead of at least two. Super 500 is one of the levels of tournament on badminton's world tour. Lakshya beat a home player in Japan to reach the last four.
in-lakshya.ask: Should young athletes play in as many tournaments as possible, or play fewer and rest more between them?

in-pinkline.ctx: Metro lines carry passengers on their own tracks, away from road traffic. This 7.5 km elevated stretch is the first part of the Pink Line to open, and it links with another line at Jayadeva Hospital station. Bengaluru's metro network is now more than 100 km long.
in-pinkline.ask: Should cities spend more on metro lines, which take years to build, or on buses, which can start running much sooner?

in-harmanpreet.ctx: India's women won their first ODI World Cup in November 2025, with Harmanpreet Kaur as captain. She has since stepped down as captain. She compared the win with 1983, the year India's men first won the World Cup.
in-harmanpreet.ask: Do statues and honours for sports stars inspire children to play, or would the money and attention do more good spent on training young players?

in-odi-nz.ctx: In an ODI each team can bat for up to 50 overs, and a team is all out when 10 batters have been dismissed. India lead the five-match series 2-1, so even if New Zealand win on Sunday, the series would end level.
in-odi-nz.ask: After a heavy defeat, should a team change several players for the next match, or keep faith in the same side?

g-popmaths.ctx: The 1960 paper used estimates of world population going back 2,000 years. Its curve only worked while growth kept speeding up. Growth peaked in the early 1960s, soon after the paper came out, so the prediction began to drift away from reality.
g-popmaths.ask: Is it helpful for scientists to use bold, dramatic predictions to get attention for a problem, or can that make people trust science less?

g-poisontips.ctx: Bones of hippos and buffalo show that this part of Arabia, now a sandy desert, once had a large lake and plenty of water. The lake existed about 125,000 years ago. The poison evidence comes from traces on the stone points, which is why the scientists say they could be, rather than are, the oldest poisoned weapons.
g-poisontips.ask: Should scientists announce a possible 'oldest ever' find before they are completely sure, or wait for more proof?

g-kane.ctx: The Nations League is a competition for European national teams. England's win took them into the quarter-finals, and Sunday's match against Spain in Madrid decides who wins the group. Kane passed Peter Shilton, a goalkeeper, to set the new men's record.
g-kane.ask: Which is more impressive for a footballer: playing a record number of games for their country, or scoring a record number of goals?

g-nkflag.ctx: A fixed ratio means every copy of a flag, small or large, has exactly the same shape. North Korea's new ratio appears in its revised constitution, published on a state website. Reports say the colours and the star stay the same.
g-nkflag.ask: Should countries keep their national symbols exactly the same forever, or is it fine to update them over time?

born.name: Robert Louis Stevenson
born.what: A Scottish writer, born in Edinburgh. He wrote the adventure story Treasure Island.

born.name: Maharaja Ranjit Singh
born.what: The founder and first maharaja of the Sikh Empire. He was known as Sher-e-Punjab, the Lion of Punjab.

days.name: World Kindness Day
days.what: A day for kind acts, big and small, held every year on 13 November. It was started in 1998 by the World Kindness Movement.

today.week: Children's Day in India is tomorrow, Saturday 14 November. The Leonid meteor shower peaks on the night of 17 to 18 November.

x.t: Rome's walls at the edge of the empire
b: Long ago, the Romans ruled a huge empire. It reached from Britain all the way to northern Africa.
In the north of England, Roman soldiers built a wall from coast to coast. It is called Hadrian's Wall and it is 118 km long.
Later they built another wall further north, in Scotland. It was made of turf, which is earth with grass on it. The Romans kept that wall for only about 20 years.
x.remember: The Romans built two great walls across Britain, at the edge of their empire.
x.q: What was the wall in Scotland made of?

o.t: Rome's walls at the edge of the empire
b: The Roman Empire was at its largest in the early 100s AD, under the emperor Trajan. It stretched from Britain in the north to northern Africa in the south, and east as far as the Euphrates River.
In northern England, the emperor Hadrian ordered a wall from coast to coast. Building began around AD 122. Hadrian's Wall ran for 118 km (73 miles) and was built mainly by soldiers.

The next emperor, Antoninus Pius, pushed further north. Around AD 142 his army began the Antonine Wall across central Scotland, from the Firth of Forth to the River Clyde. It was about 60 km long and made of turf, with a deep ditch in front. The Romans held it for only about 20 years. Both walls are now part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
At Vindolanda, a fort just south of Hadrian's Wall, people left letters written in ink on thin pieces of wood. One, about 1,900 years old, is an invitation to a birthday party.
o.remember: Hadrian's Wall: begun about AD 122, 118 km long. Antonine Wall: begun about AD 142, about 60 km long, made of turf.
o.q: Which emperor's army built the wall across central Scotland?

steps.o: Cars, factories, farm fires and firecrackers all put smoke into the air.
steps.x: Cars, fires and firecrackers put smoke into the air.

steps.o: On cold, still nights a layer of warm air settles above the city and acts like a lid.
steps.x: On cold, still nights, warm air sits on top like a lid.

steps.o: The smoke cannot rise, so it spreads sideways and builds up as smog. Wind or rain is what finally clears it.
steps.x: The smoke is stuck. It spreads out and becomes smog. Wind or rain clears it.

steps.o: A bit of space rock, often smaller than a pea, speeds towards Earth.
steps.x: A tiny space rock, smaller than a pea, flies towards Earth.

steps.o: It hits the air at tens of kilometres per second and squeezes the air in front of it. Squeezed air gets extremely hot.
steps.x: It hits the air super fast and squashes it. Squashed air gets very hot.

steps.o: The heat makes the air and the rock glow, usually 70 to 100 km up. From the ground you see a bright streak.
steps.x: The hot air and rock glow. From the ground you see a bright streak!

steps.o: Throw a ball from a tall tower and gravity curves it down to the ground.
steps.x: Throw a ball. It curves down and lands.

steps.o: Throw it faster and it lands further away, because the ground curves away beneath it while it falls.
steps.x: Throw it faster. It lands further away, because Earth is round.

steps.o: At about 28,000 km an hour it falls around Earth and never lands. That endless fall is an orbit, and it is how satellites stay up.
steps.x: Go fast enough and it keeps falling around Earth without landing. That is an orbit!

steps.o: Sunlight passes through the air and warms the land and the sea.
steps.x: Sunlight comes down and warms the Earth.

steps.o: The warm Earth sends heat back up. Much of it escapes into space, which keeps the planet from overheating.
steps.x: The warm Earth sends heat back up into space.

steps.o: Gases such as carbon dioxide, from burning coal, oil and gas, act like a blanket. They trap more of the heat, so the planet slowly warms.
steps.x: Gases from burning coal, oil and gas act like a blanket. They keep more heat in, so Earth gets warmer.

hiddenWords.o: Emperor comes from the Latin word imperator, which meant commander. It grew from the verb imperare, to command. The word came into English through French and has been used since the 1200s.
Archaeology comes from the Greek word arkhaios, meaning ancient. The Greek word arkhaiologia meant the study of ancient things. The word has been used in English since about 1600.

backThen.t: Rabindranath Tagore is named winner of the Nobel Prize
backThen.o: On this day in 1913, the Nobel Prize in Literature was announced for the poet Rabindranath Tagore, who was born in Calcutta in 1861. He was the first person from outside Europe to win it. The prize praised his "profoundly sensitive, fresh and beautiful verse". His book of poems Gitanjali was among the work that won him the prize.
backThen.x: On this day in 1913, a poet from India was named winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature. His name was Rabindranath Tagore. No one from outside Europe had won it before!
backThen.why: It was the first time the literature prize went to a writer from outside Europe. The prize said Tagore had made his poetry, in his own English words, part of the literature of the West.

bigStory.t: Can the world agree to slow climate change?
bigStory.sub: COP31, the United Nations climate summit in Türkiye

x.why: Almost 200 countries are in one place to decide how to stop Earth getting too warm. What they agree will shape the world you grow up in.

o.why: Almost 200 countries are in one place to decide how to turn climate promises into action. What they agree, or fail to agree, will shape the world you grow up in.

facts: the limit countries hope to keep to
where current promises lead, says a UN report
the day the talks are due to end

days.o: COP31 opened in Antalya, a city on Türkiye's coast. In an unusual setup, Türkiye is the host while Australia leads the negotiations.
days.x: The big meeting began in Antalya, a city by the sea in Türkiye. Türkiye is the host, and Australia is leading the talks.

days.o: UN Secretary-General António Guterres urged leaders to get serious. A UN report projects about 2.6°C of warming this century on current promises, well above the Paris Agreement goal.
days.x: The leader of the United Nations asked every country to get serious. A report says Earth is on track to warm more than countries promised.

days.o: Leaders gather today and tomorrow. Organisers call this the implementation COP: less about new promises, more about keeping old ones. The United States did not send officials.
days.x: Presidents and prime ministers arrive today. This meeting is about keeping old promises, and less about making new ones.

days.o: On the first day of speeches, UN chief António Guterres said the climate crisis is outrunning us. Türkiye asked countries to back a voluntary pledge to raise electricity's share of the world's energy use from about 23 per cent to 35 per cent by 2035. The head of the European Commission backed it. Others want it to say the electricity must be clean.
days.x: Leaders gave speeches. The head of the United Nations said the world must move faster. Türkiye asked countries to run more cars, homes and factories on electricity.

days.o: Leaders gave their speeches and went home. At least 14 countries have publicly backed the electricity pledge, by one news site's count, and a climate fund announced 94 million dollars to help developing countries electrify. But a fund for Pacific islands and a fund for tropical forests are still short of their targets, and countries still disagree about money for adapting to climate change. In week two, negotiators must agree a final text. The summit is due to end on 20 November.
days.x: Leaders gave their speeches and went home. Some countries promised to run more things on electricity. Others asked for more money to help. Next week, countries must agree on a plan.

poll.q: If you were a leader at COP31, what would you push for first?
a: Most warming comes from burning coal, oil and gas for energy, so this is where the biggest cuts are.
Trees take carbon dioxide out of the air, and forests are home to most land animals.
Helping places hit by floods and heat
Poorer countries have done the least to cause warming and are often hit hardest.
Cars, lorries, ships and planes burn a lot of fuel. Electric and shared travel cut that.
